query: Given a CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy where conventional casting yields porosity and a homogeneous but soft single-phase structure, and where previous attempts suffered from low hardness, propose a solid-state processing strategy involving high-energy milling followed by rapid sintering. The target is to suppress porosity while driving the formation of a fine-grained nanocrystalline solid solution (dominated by FCC with minor BCC) rather than a brittle HCP phase often associated with Titanium-rich systems. Incorporate known constraints on displacement rates and thermal expansion during sintering into the hypothesis. Define the operating regime (temperature/strain rate) where this dual-phase stability is maximized, and propose a specific mechanical test (e.g., indentation load and dwell time) that would falsify the claim that the observed hardness is due to grain refinement rather than solute strengthening.

generation.target_system: CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy (HEA) processed via high-energy ball milling followed by rapid spark plasma sintering (SPS), targeting a fine-grained nanocrystalline dual-phase (FCC + minor BCC) solid solution with suppressed porosity.

However, the specific phase evolution (BCC to FCC oxide) differs from the target's FCC/BCC solid solution goal, requiring derivation of the phase stability mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: By employing high-energy ball milling (HEBM) for 10 hours followed by rapid spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 900–1000 °C with a heating rate >100 °C/min and a dwell time of <5 minutes, the CoCrFeNiTi alloy will achieve near-theoretical density (>98%) and a nanocrystalline microstructure (grain size 20–50 nm). The rapid thermal cycle will suppress the diffusion-driven formation of brittle HCP or complex intermetallic phases (often associated with Ti-rich regions) and stabilize a dual-phase solid solution dominated by FCC with a minor BCC fraction. The high stacking fault energy (SFE) of the CoCrFeNiTi system at these temperatures, combined with the solute strengthening from Ti and the grain boundary strengthening from the nanocrystalline structure, will yield a hardness of 450–550 HV. The operating regime for dual-phase stability is defined by a temperature window (900–1000 °C) where the FCC phase is thermodynamically favored over HCP (due to entropy stabilization and SFE) but below the threshold for significant grain coarsening or Laves phase precipitation. To falsify the claim that hardness is due to grain refinement rather than solute strengthening, a nanoindentation test will be performed with a load of 10 mN and a dwell time of 10 seconds. If the hardness remains constant (>450 HV) when the grain size is artificially increased to >1 µm via annealing at 1100 °C for 1 hour (while maintaining the same composition), the claim that hardness is primarily due to grain refinement will be falsified, confirming solute strengthening as the dominant mechanism.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNiTi powder mixture (equimolar or near-equimolar) with potential for Ti segregation and oxide contamination if milled for excessive durations.
generation.intervention: High-energy ball milling for 10 hours in a protective Ar atmosphere to achieve nanocrystalline powder with minimal contamination, followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 900–1000 °C with a heating rate >100 °C/min and a dwell time <5 minutes.
generation.conditions: Temperature: 900–1000 °C; Heating rate: >100 °C/min; Dwell time: <5 min; Atmosphere: High vacuum or high-purity Ar; Displacement rate: Controlled to prevent excessive thermal expansion mismatch (target <10 µm/s during heating ramp).
generation.structural_mediator: Nanocrystalline grain boundaries (20–50 nm) and a dual-phase FCC/BCC solid solution matrix stabilized by high configurational entropy and solute drag.
generation.mechanism: The mechanism relies on the suppression of HCP phase formation via rapid thermal processing (SPS) which limits the time available for Ti-driven HCP nucleation, coupled with the stabilization of the FCC phase by the high configurational entropy of the CoCrFeNiTi system (derived from PMC6093928 principles on SFE and temperature dependence). The hardness is driven by a combination of grain boundary strengthening (Hall-Petch effect) from the nanocrystalline structure and solute strengthening from Ti and other elements. The rapid sintering prevents grain coarsening and the formation of brittle intermetallics (Laves or HCP) that typically occur in slower cooling or higher temperature regimes (derived from PMC7866258 and PMC8510135 constraints on milling time and temperature).
generation.predicted_outcome: A dense (>98%) bulk alloy with a nanocrystalline (20–50 nm) dual-phase (FCC dominant, minor BCC) microstructure, exhibiting a hardness of 450–550 HV, compressive yield strength >1500 MPa, and ductility >10% (due to FCC dominance), with no significant porosity or brittle HCP phases.
generation.baseline: Conventional casting yields a homogeneous but soft single-phase structure with porosity and low hardness (<200 HV) due to coarse grains and lack of solid solution strengthening.
generation.boundary: The strategy fails if milling time exceeds 15 hours (leading to excessive contamination and oxide formation) or if sintering temperature exceeds 1100 °C (leading to grain coarsening and HCP/Laves phase precipitation). The dual-phase stability is lost if the cooling rate is too slow, allowing HCP nucleation.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty exists regarding the exact Ti content threshold for HCP suppression in the CoCrFeNiTi system without Mn, as the SFE of CoCrFeNiTi may differ from CoCrFeMnNi. The precise sintering temperature window (900–1000 °C) may need fine-tuning based on the specific Ti content to avoid Laves phase formation. The hardness prediction assumes no significant oxide contamination, which is sensitive to milling media wear.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CoCrFeNiTi samples: Set A (as-processed via MA+SPS) and Set B (Set A annealed at 1100 °C for 1 hour to coarsen grains to >1 µm while maintaining composition). Perform nanoindentation on both sets.
measurements: Hardness (HV) at 10 mN load, 10 s dwell time
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the hardness of Set B (coarse-grained) is statistically indistinguishable from Set A (nanocrystalline) and remains >450 HV, the claim that hardness is primarily due to grain refinement is falsified, indicating solute strengthening is the dominant mechanism. Conversely, if hardness drops significantly in Set B, grain refinement is confirmed as the primary driver.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract High entropy alloys based on 3d transition metals display rich and promising magnetic characteristics for various high-technology applications. Understanding their behavior at finite temperature is, however, limited by the incomplete experimental data for single-phase alloys. Here we use first-principles alloy theory to investigate the magnetic structure of polymorphic CoCrFeMnNi in the paramagnetic state by accounting for the longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) as a function of temperature. In both face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures, the LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr and Ni. The impact of LSFs is demonstrated on the phase stability, stacking fault energy and the fcc-hcp interfacial energy. The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions. With increasing temperature, the stacking fault energy increases, suppressing the formation of stacking faults and nano-twins. Our predictions are consistent with recent experimental findings.

Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening. This paper reports the microstructural evolution and mechanical properties of a low-density Al 0.3 NbTa 0.8 Ti 1.5 V 0.2 Zr refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) prepared by means of a combination of mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering (SPS). Prior to sintering, the morphology, chemical homogeneity and crystal structures of the powders were thoroughly investigated by varying the milling times to find optimal conditions for densification. The sintered bulk RHEAs were produced with diverse feedstock powder conditions. The microstructural development of the materials was analyzed in terms of phase composition and constitution, chemical homogeneity, and crystallographic properties. Hardness and elastic constants also were measured. The calculation of phase diagrams (CALPHAD) was performed to predict the phase changes in the alloy, and the results were compared with the experiments. Milling time seems to play a significant role in the contamination level of the sintered materials. Abstract This work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe) 2 O 4 /Fe(Co,Cr) 2 O 4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples. Processed samples rich in grain boundaries (GBs) promote internal oxidation to form Al-rich inner oxides.
